summary: OAuth 2.0 authorization requests normally carry parameters in the URI sent through the browser, so they can be tampered with, are not source-authenticated and can be observed. This document lets request parameters be sent in a JSON Web Token instead, which can be signed and encrypted. The request can be sent by value or by reference.

eli5.summary: A note passed between people through a middle person can be changed or read. Here the note is sealed in a signed, locked envelope, so nobody can change it.

questions: what is a request object in oauth
how to sign an oauth authorization request
subtitle: Put an OAuth 2.0 authorization request inside a signed (and optionally encrypted) JWT instead of plain URL parameters.

tldr.problem: OAuth 2.0 authorization requests travel as URI query parameters through the browser, so they are not integrity protected, the sender is not authenticated, and they can be monitored.
tldr.mechanism: The request parameters go into a JWT called a Request Object, signed with JWS and optionally encrypted with JWE, and sent either by value in the request parameter or by reference in the request_uri parameter.
tldr.outcome: The authorization server can check who sent the request and that it was not changed. The RFC adds new error codes, metadata values and security guidance for the by-reference method.

facts.label: Request URI randomness
facts.value: 128 bits or more, valid under a minute

today: RFC 9101 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2021. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and builds on RFC 6749.

sections.title: Why Plain OAuth Requests Fall Short
sections.content:
In OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) the authorization request is serialized into the query of a URI and sent through a user agent such as a web browser. Parameters like response_type, client_id, state and redirect_uri sit in plain view in that URI.

TLS protects each hop, but TLS sessions end in the user agent and may also end early at a middlebox such as a load balancer. The RFC lists three resulting weaknesses:

  • The request is not integrity protected, so parameters can be tainted.
  • The source of the request is not authenticated.
  • The request can be monitored on its way.

These weaknesses have enabled attacks such as redirection URI rewriting. Application-layer security also lets a trusted third party prepare a request, so a client cannot ask for more permissions than were agreed. The RFC notes that this capability is already in use by OpenID Connect.
sections.eli5: Today the request is like a postcard handed to a stranger to carry. Anyone along the way could read it, change it or pretend to be the sender.

sections.title: The Request Object
sections.content:
A Request Object is a JSON Web Token (JWT) whose claims set holds the OAuth 2.0 authorization request parameters. It MUST contain all the parameters used to process the request, including extension parameters, except request and request_uri, which must not appear inside it. Names and string values are JSON strings encoded in UTF-8, and numbers are JSON numbers.

The object is signed with JWS. If signed, it SHOULD contain the claims iss and aud, where aud should be the authorization server's issuer from RFC 8414. To also encrypt it, the JWT MUST be signed first and then encrypted with JWE, giving a Nested JWT. A Request Object must therefore be either JWS signed, or JWS signed and JWE encrypted.

The client picks the algorithms, which both sides must support. They can announce what they support through dynamic client registration metadata (RFC 7591) and authorization server metadata (RFC 8414). The media type is application/oauth-authz-req+jwt, though some deployments may use application/jwt.

The RFC's example claims include iss, aud, response_type, client_id, redirect_uri, scope, state and the extension parameters nonce and max_age, signed with RS256.
sections.eli5: The request is written on a card, stamped with the sender's own seal, and can also be put in a locked box. The seal shows who wrote it and that nobody changed it.

sections.title: Sending the Request: By Value or By Reference
sections.content:
The client builds the authorization URI by adding parameters to the authorization endpoint's query:

  • request: the Request Object itself. Required unless request_uri is used, and the two MUST NOT both appear.
  • request_uri: an absolute URI that points to the Request Object. Required unless request is used.
  • client_id: always required, and it MUST match the client_id in the Request Object.

The client may also repeat the parameters in the query for backward compatibility, but a server that supports this specification MUST use only the parameters in the Request Object.

By value puts the whole object in request. By reference lets the server fetch the object from the request_uri. This helps when the request would be large, since signing and especially public-key cryptography add size, and when the client does not want to do application-level cryptography itself.

The whole Request URI SHOULD NOT exceed 512 ASCII characters, because many phones accept only 512 or 1024 characters and large URLs are slow on a 2G connection. If the server must fetch from a URI the client supplied, it is an https URI; if the URI came from the authorization server itself, it MUST be a URN.

The server MUST send an HTTP GET to retrieve the object, unless it can securely retrieve it another way. The request_uri MUST have enough entropy that it cannot be guessed, and it is RECOMMENDED that it be removed after a reasonable timeout unless access control is used.
sections.eli5: You can hand over the sealed note directly, or hand over a slip saying where the note is kept. The slip is shorter, but the server then has to go and fetch the note.

sections.title: Validating and Answering a JWT Request
sections.content:
If the object is encrypted, the authorization server MUST decrypt it per the JWE specification. If decryption fails, it MUST return an invalid_request_object error.

It MUST then validate the JWS signature. If a kid header is present, that key MUST be used and MUST belong to the client. Algorithm verification follows RFC 8725. If the key is not associated with the client, or the signature fails, the server MUST return invalid_request_object.

The server extracts the parameters from the Request Object only, even if the same parameter is in the query, and the two client_id values MUST be identical. It then validates the request as in RFC 6749; failures return an error as in Section 5.2 of that RFC.

Responses are created as in RFC 6749. This document adds four error values:

  • invalid_request_uri: the request_uri returns an error or invalid data.
  • invalid_request_object: the request contains an invalid Request Object.
  • request_not_supported: the server does not support request.
  • request_uri_not_supported: the server does not support request_uri.

Clients supporting the request_uri method MUST support TLS following RFC 7525 and verify the server certificate using DNS-ID (RFC 6125); the CN field must not be used for authentication.
sections.eli5: The server opens the lock, checks the seal belongs to the right sender, and trusts only what is written on the note, not whatever is scribbled on the outside.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The request source MUST always be verified, most reliably by checking the JWS signature. Encrypting to a public key does not authenticate the sender, because anyone can encrypt to a public key. When the authorization server offers a service that swaps a Request Object for a URI, it MUST authenticate the client, bind the client identifier to the URI, and validate the signature. Such a URI can be replayed, so its lifetime MUST be short and preferably one-time; the guidance is under a minute and at least 128 bits of cryptographic randomness.

Risks tied to request_uri:

  • DDoS: malicious clients can point it at huge or slow content, or at another request_uri to cause recursive lookups. Servers should check the location, check that the media type is application/oauth-authz-req+jwt, use a timeout and not follow recursive fetches.
  • URI rewrite: the request_uri value is not signed, so a man-in-the-browser can alter it to request extra scope or aim a DoS at a victim.

Downgrade: an attacker could fall back to plain RFC 6749 requests. The RFC defines the boolean metadata value require_signed_request_object for both clients and servers (default false). When true, the server MUST reject non-conforming requests and requests using alg of none.

Other points: the two client_id values must match to guard against parameter mismatches. For cross-JWT confusion, avoid using the client ID as sub, optionally use explicit typing with typ set to oauth-authz-req+jwt, or use distinct signing keys. The RFC warns that requiring explicit typing would break most existing deployments.
sections.eli5: A sealed note is only safe if the receiver always insists on the seal, and a pointer to a note needs care: it must be hard to guess, quick to expire and not be a trap for the server.

sections.title: Privacy Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to RFC 6973 for privacy guidance and notes only what is specific to this design. A trusted third party can help with collection limitation: it examines a client's business process, certifies which claims it needs, and issues a client credential. The client then uses that credential to push Request Objects to the third party and get a request_uri. The consent screen MUST indicate the client and SHOULD say the request was vetted.

For disclosure limitation, query parameters can leak through referrers and browser history, so if a request holds sensitive parameters the client SHOULD encrypt the Request Object with JWE. Persistent per-user request URIs could be used to track a user, so they should be avoided, and single-use URIs are one alternative.
sections.eli5: A trusted referee can check that an app only asks for what it really needs. Sealing the note also keeps nosy people from reading it, and each claim slip should be used once so nobody can follow you around with it.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: Because a Request Object is a JWT, the core JWT claims cannot be reused for other meanings inside it. The RFC therefore registers them, starting with iss and sub, as OAuth authorization request parameters in the OAuth Parameters registry, along with the new request and request_uri parameters. It also adds authorization server metadata and dynamic client registration metadata entries for the request object algorithm values, and registers the media type application/oauth-authz-req+jwt.
sections.eli5: The official lists are updated so these new names have one clear meaning for everybody.
